Speed, support recovery and reproducible benchmarks

Source: vignettes/articles/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd

L0glm’s shrinking active set, compiled solvers and fast GIC preset can deliver striking gains in both speed and support recovery. These examples compare complete fitting and selection workflows. Each table identifies the tuning rule, and reports support recovery separately from elapsed time. The deconvolution examples use the website benchmark. The million-predictor comparison reproduces the LASSO workflows. The README and this page share the same published measurements.

One million predictor example

The design has 500 observations, one million standard-normal predictors and 60 nonzero coefficients of either sign. L0glm uses GIC-preset ISIS plus a relaxed refit. LASSO and fully relaxed LASSO are tuned by BIC or five-fold CV on the unscreened design. The screening tutorial compares complete models when all methods use SIS or ISIS.

Method Selection Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC
L0glm + ISIS GIC preset 6.52 2579 40 2 20 999938 0.784 0.797
LASSO BIC path 23.42 14789 23 612 37 999328 0.066 0.118
Relaxed LASSO BIC path 22.47 10588 21 453 39 999487 0.079 0.124
LASSO 5-fold CV 120.69 4309 17 50 43 999890 0.268 0.268
Relaxed LASSO 5-fold CV 99.24 7413 20 252 40 999688 0.120 0.156

Fast fitting and selection, higher sensitivity and fewer false positives in the million-predictor example. L0glm uses a GIC preset; both LASSO methods use five-fold CV. There are 60 true effects.

In this simulation L0glm is 19 times faster than five-fold-CV LASSO and recovers more true effects with fewer false positives. The L0glm timing includes screening and one preset fit; the other methods evaluate up to 40 native path values, with paths refitted in each CV training fold. BIC is shown alongside CV because GIC can select a null LASSO model at this dimension. All rows retain GIC as a common evaluation score. Five-fold comparisons use the same random folds.

Simulation is excluded from timings. The documented run uses one BLAS thread and eight screening threads; the design is held in memory. The L0glm time is the median of three runs. The common-scoring CV implementation used for the LASSO rows evaluates folds serially. Standalone benchmarks that call cv.glmnet() use parallel folds through cv_glmnet_parallel(). See the million-predictor tutorial for the complete data setup.

Simulations from the abess documentation

The abess power tutorial uses Gaussian and logistic regression with 1,000 predictors and ten true effects. We use its generator for both families. The low-correlation design is AR(1) with parameter 0.1. The high-correlation design has pairwise correlation 0.7. Each family and correlation setting uses ten independent simulations and a fresh test set of the same size as the training set. There are 500 observations per Gaussian dataset and 1,000 per logistic dataset.

L0glm uses the GIC preset, a relaxed refit and the default automatic local support refinement. The other methods select from their fitted paths using the common GIC in sparseGLM(). ABESS searches support sizes 0 to 60. The other paths use up to 40 values. These are GIC comparisons on the abess simulation designs. The abess tutorial uses a different tuning protocol. Test RMSE or AUC, sensitivity, false-positive rate and MCC are means over the ten replications. Seconds are median elapsed fitting and selection time with one BLAS thread. L0glm recovers all ten Gaussian effects on average, with test RMSE close to the noise standard deviation of one, in about a quarter of a second. L0Learn is faster on these Gaussian designs, while L0glm takes about half the time of ABESS. In the strongly correlated logistic design, L0glm recovers 82% of the true effects with a 0.09% false-positive rate and MCC 0.862, taking 1.07 s. ABESS recovers 84% with a 0.37% false-positive rate and MCC 0.775, taking 2.04 s. L0Learn gives the highest test AUC there. Support recovery and prediction measure different aspects of these fitted models.

Single channel deconvolution

A realistic blurred Poisson spike train has 10,000 observations, 10,000 predictors and 1,000 true peaks. Every fit is evaluated using the original Poisson likelihood and a common GIC.

Method Selection Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC
L0glm GIC preset 0.14 102682 845 154 155 8846 0.845 0.828
LASSO GIC path 0.24 145904 950 2096 50 6904 0.470 0.467
Relaxed LASSO GIC path 0.42 122083 905 999 95 8001 0.623 0.607
LASSO 5-fold CV 2.72 146234 951 2146 49 6854 0.464 0.462
Relaxed LASSO 5-fold CV 2.77 133122 920 1523 80 7477 0.534 0.524

L0glm uses one GIC preset with a relaxed refit. LASSO and relaxed LASSO search ten explicit lambda values using GIC or five-fold CV, with a weighted-Gaussian approximation and observation weights 1/(y+0.1). CV selects glmnet’s minimum weighted prediction error using four parallel workers. ABESS is omitted from this large example. The deconvolution tutorial shows mirrored signals and true-versus-estimated coefficient plots.

Multichannel deconvolution

The GC/MS-style simulation also has 10,000 rows, 10,000 candidate peak locations and 1,000 true peaks, with all 226 informative mass channels retained. Shared chromatographic peak times correspond to active coefficient rows; within-row coefficients describe the mass spectra.

Method Selection Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC Within-row F1 Within-row MCC
L0glm GIC preset 8.03 5606331 944 11 56 8989 0.966 0.962 0.912 0.869
Group LASSO GIC path 201.03 7413616 980 860 20 8140 0.690 0.685 0.842 0.768
Relaxed group LASSO GIC path 804.89 6138687 909 309 91 8691 0.820 0.802 0.853 0.782
Group LASSO 5-fold CV 593.23 9639345 998 4242 2 4758 0.320 0.316 0.886 0.830
Relaxed group LASSO 5-fold CV 2460.38 6198648 962 502 38 8498 0.781 0.769 0.856 0.785

Row F1 and MCC measure peak recovery. Within-row F1 and MCC assess spectral sparsity among correctly recovered true-positive peaks. L0glm uses the full Poisson likelihood with channel-specific working weights. Grouped glmnet uses shared row weights 1/(rowMeans(y)+0.1) for its labelled Gaussian approximation. GIC selection scores ten lambda values using the original Poisson likelihood; five-fold CV selects the minimum weighted prediction error on the same lambda grid. Fully relaxed fits use gamma=0. L0glm uses lambda="gic" and four outcome-fitting threads; CV uses four parallel workers. Timings include the complete fitting and selection workflow, including worker startup for CV. The preset time is the median of three runs with matching coefficients. Simulation and final metric reporting are excluded.

The deconvolution tutorial stacks observed data, ground truth and fitted coefficient heatmaps, and shows all-channel coefficient comparisons in a single column.

Local support refinement

local.search refines a completed adaptive-ridge fit by testing predictor additions, deletions and small exchanges. Its parameter-count objective uses the same conventions as GIC() and the tuning functions. The default "auto" applies the search to initial supports with at most 50 coefficient dimensions, after any SIS/ISIS screening. The reference gives the computational-size rule, controls and returned diagnostics.

fit <- l0glmFit(X, y, family=binomial(), lambda="gic",
  local.search="auto")
fit$local.search$history

The paired comparison below uses the same 40 datasets as the abess-design benchmark: ten replications for each family and correlation. GIC, TP, FP and MCC are means; timings are medians. Both variants use the same GIC preset and relaxed fitting option. Elapsed time here measures l0glmFit() itself; the nine-method comparison includes the common sparseGLM() scoring workflow. Model selection uses only the training data.

Family Correlation Local search GIC TP FP MCC Seconds
Gaussian 0.1 FALSE 1799.1 9.5 0.0 0.974 0.05
Gaussian 0.1 auto 1563.5 10.0 0.8 0.964 0.19
Gaussian 0.7 FALSE 1767.5 9.5 0.0 0.974 0.05
Gaussian 0.7 auto 1563.1 10.0 0.4 0.982 0.18
Logistic 0.1 FALSE 362.7 9.8 0.0 0.990 0.12
Logistic 0.1 auto 357.4 10.0 0.6 0.973 0.51
Logistic 0.7 FALSE 320.3 3.7 2.1 0.482 0.17
Logistic 0.7 auto 222.0 8.2 0.9 0.862 0.96

The refinement substantially improves Gaussian prediction and recovery of correlated logistic effects. In the Gaussian examples, mean test RMSE falls from 1.46–1.48 to 1.02. For correlated logistic predictors, mean MCC rises from 0.482 to 0.862. The extra work is concentrated on small models: additions, deletions and exchanges are accepted only when they improve the chosen training criterion.

Reproduction script · Per-run comparisons

Large multichannel deconvolution models exceed this automatic size limit. Their initial coefficients are retained. TRUE explicitly requests refinement for larger supports, and FALSE disables it.

For example, a 10,000-predictor, 228-channel Poisson control fit took 5.73 s with "auto" and 5.85 s with FALSE, with identical coefficients. Explicitly requesting three search rounds improved GIC from 5,525,411 to 5,494,470 and within-row MCC from 0.870 to 0.878, taking 34.36 s. The default size limit preserves the fast fitting path for models of this size. Run benchmark_local_deconvolution() from the reproduction script to repeat these deconvolution controls.

Native validation and OpenMP

Both drivers can select an IRLS checkpoint by held-out deviance. The specialized l0nnPois backend evaluates validation in native code and fits channels in parallel. This example uses 1,000 predictors, 16 channels, 60 active rows and an independent Poisson replicate for validation. Timings are medians of five fits with one BLAS thread.

Backend Outcome threads Seconds Validation deviance GIC F1 MCC
General driver 1 1.19 0.357611 42687.99 0.945 0.943
l0nnPois 1 0.10 0.357611 42687.99 0.945 0.943
l0nnPois 2 0.07 0.357611 42687.99 0.945 0.943
l0nnPois 4 0.05 0.357611 42687.99 0.945 0.943
l0nnPois 8 0.05 0.357611 42687.99 0.945 0.943

The fits agree across drivers and thread counts. Run benchmark_native_validation.R to reproduce the comparison.

Reproduce and extend

  • Website benchmark source: preset fits, comparisons and plots.
  • Million-predictor LASSO benchmark: BIC and five-fold CV comparisons.
  • Gaussian/logistic benchmark: matched comparisons with ABESS, L0Learn, LASSO variants, MCP and SCAD.
  • Local support refinement: paired comparisons with refinement enabled or disabled.
  • Solver/problem-size benchmark: solvers, families, matrix storage and sizes.
  • Single/multichannel benchmark: detailed signal examples and alternative methods.
  • sparseGLM(): use the same comparison framework on your own data.

The benchmarks were run on an HP ZBook Fury 17.3-inch G8 Mobile Workstation with an 11th-generation Intel Core i9-11950H at 2.60 GHz, 8 physical cores and 16 logical cores, running Windows and R 4.5.0 with OpenBLAS. BLAS uses one thread. Screening in the million-predictor example uses eight physical cores. Multichannel deconvolution uses four outcome-fitting threads, and deconvolution CV uses four parallel workers. Single-channel fits use one fitting thread. Timings will vary with hardware and tuning choices. F1 and MCC evaluate the known simulated support; it is never used to select models. Likelihood floors and approximation labels are explicit in the benchmark source.
